2 Abstract Copper-based metal organic frameworks (MOFs) and their derivatives have been attempted to drive CO2 electroreduction, whereas they still suffered from obvious drawbacks like poor selectivity and durability. Here, Cu_btc (btc = benzene-1,3,5tricarboxylate) derived Cu2O/Cu anchored in nitrogen doped porous carbon framework (Cu2O/Cu@NC) was prepared for CO2 electroreduction. The Cu2O/Cu@NC-800 (carbonizing Cu_btc at 800 °C) produced formate and ethanol concurrently with overpotential as low as ~380 mV. However, it exhibited higher selectivity towards formate against ethanol, with the maximum formate faradaic efficiencies 70.5 % at – 0.68 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) which was 1.79 and 1.84 times higher than that of Cu2O/Cu@NC-700 and Cu2O/Cu@NC-900. This superior performance maintained stable over 30 h. The enhancement in activity and selectivity was attributed to (i) higher Cu content and well dispersed Cu2O/Cu nanoparticles inside carbon frameworks which provided abundant active reaction sites, and (ii) higher content of N doped into the Cu2O/Cu lattice to possibly facilitated *OCHO generation. These findings provided a convenient strategy to enhance the activity and selectivity of catalysts for efficient CO2 electroreduction. Keywords CO2 electroreduction; Cu2O/Cu; Nitrogen-doped carbon frameworks; Core-shell structure; Formate selectivity; Durability

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The extended depletion of traditional fossil fuels and the resulting emission of CO2 have given rise to worldwide energy crisis and global warming. 1-3 Concerning these serious problems, different methods to capture, stabilize or convert CO2 have caused great research interests. 4 Electrochemically reducing CO2 into value-added chemicals provided an attractive route for producing sustainably industrial feedstocks and relieving the CO2 level in the atmosphere. 4-6 This complex electro-reduction process involved multiple proton and electron transfer steps, making it possible for generating a variety of products like carbon monoxide, hydrocarbon, carboxylic acid, and alcohols when used the most promising copper-based electrodes. 2, 7-8 Although extensive efforts have been involed in tuning the morphology and structure of copper-based catalysts to improve the catalytic activity, 9-14 some severe challenges like large overpotential and poor selectivity still existed. It was urgent to design a catalyst with higher energy efficiency, selectivity, and durability. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), built by organic linkers and metal-rich nodes, were characterized by large specific surface area, high porosity, and tunable pore size. 15-16 Such structure created a possible way to provide well-separated active sites within the framework which rendered it to be an excellent catalysts precursors for electrochemical reduction of CO2. 17-19 Up to now, a series of catalysts like Cu-, 20-22 Fe-, 23 Co-, 24-25 Zn-, 26 Zr-, 27-28 and Re-MOFs 29 have been tested to drive the CO2 electrochemical reduction. Thanks to the unique capability to selectively produce hydrocarbons and oxygenates, Cu-MOFs have attracted remarkable interest with regard

4 to electrochemically converting CO2 to some organics. Hinogami et al. 20 first evaluated the performance of Cu(II) rubeanate framework for CO2 electroconversion. This MOF catalyst outperformed Cu electrode in the tested potential range, which was attributed to the relatively weak adsorption of CO2 on the ionic Cu(II) sites. Although the formic acid was 13 times higher compared to that on Cu electrode at –1.2 V vs. standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), only 30% faradaic efficiency (FE) was achieved. Cu3(BTC)2 coating on glassy carbon electrode was also used for CO2 reduction in an CO2-saturated electrolyte consisting of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) solution of tetrabutylammonium tetrafluoroborate. In this non-aqueous solvent, FE for oxalic acid reached 51%. 21 Although oxide-derived Cu/carbon (OD Cu/C) by carbonizating Cubased MOFs in an inert atmosphere 30 favored the production of methanol, ethanol, and formic acid, the relatively poor selectivity still needed to be further improved. Based on these works, it was easy to find that the activity and selectivity of these Cu-MOF electro-catalysts towards CO2 electroreduction was far from satisfactory in the aqueous electrolyte. It is concluded that the electrocatalytic performance of catalysts for CO2 reduction depended on the intrinsic property of the metal, morphologic and structural charateristics of metal particles and carbon substrate. 30 MOFs, as one of the attractive precursors, could be used to fabricate the hybrid catalystes containing metal (oxides) nanoparticles and porous carbon materials. In addition, various heteroatoms (e.g., N, S, and P, etc.) could be efficiently introduced into the carbon structure by choosing different modulators. 31 In this way, the chemical, electrical, and functional properties

This was strengthened by the higher FE for CO2-to-CO conversion with N-doped carbon nanotubes and a linear increment of FECO with the N content in N-doped carbon nanotubes. 32 It was also speculated that nitrogen doping could change the electronic structure of copper-based reaction sites 33 which improved the activity and selectivity for CO2 electroreduction. Based on these results, MOFsderived metal (oxide) anchored in N-doped porous carbon would be a promising candidate for CO2 electroreduction with high selectivity and activity. In this study, we prepared a benzimidazole modified Cu-btc as a sacrificial template to prepare the Cu2O/Cu nanospheres anchored in nitrogen-doped porous carbon hybrid composites (Cu2O/Cu@NC). Due to the unique structure, the Cu2O/Cu@NC composites exhibited a big improvement of activity, selectivity, and durability for electrochemical CO2-to-formate conversion. The structure property, the N-doping species and content in catalyst composites, and the electrosorption activities were discussed to illustrate the main reason for the increased performance.

Copper (II) nitrate hydrate (Cu(NO3)2 · 3H2O), 1,3,5-Benzenetricarboxylic acid (H3BTC), benzimidazole, ethanol, and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Chemical Co. The bright blue solution was acquired after mixing the two solutions which was further stirred for 15 min. At the same time, 0.1 mmol H3BTC was also dissolved in 9 mL ethanol and 9 mL DMF, this solution was then mixed with the above mixture and agitated for 6 h at 90 oC. After the reaction, the products were centrifuged and washed with ethanol and finally dried at 60 oC. Preparation of Cu2O/Cu@NC: Porous Cu2O/Cu@NC materials were prepared via the carbonization of the obtained Cu_btc precursors at different temperature (700, 800, and 900 oC) for 5 h in high purity Ar atmosphere with a heating rate of 2 °C min–1.

sections.heading: 2.4 Electrochemical performance
sections.text:
Preparation of electrode: 24 mg catalyst was mixed with 640 μL mL of isopropyl alcohol and 172 μL of Nafion solution (5.0 wt%) and then the mixture was maintained in an ultrasonic bath for 1 h. After that, the prepared ink was brushed onto a carbon cloth with an area of 6 cm2 (2 cm × 3 cm), followed by drying at 30 °C under vacuum condition. Electrochemical activities test: A gastight H-type dual chamber cell (separated by a Nafion 117 proton exchange membrane) was used to test the electrochemical performance of electrodes. The as-prepared electrodes and a platinum gauze (1 cm2) as the working electrode and counter electrode were placed in each chamber, an Ag/AgCl electrode (saturated KCl, +197 mV vs. standard hydrogen electrode) as the reference electrode was fixed with working electrode with 0.5 cm of distance. All the tested potentials were against reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) by VRHE=VAg/AgCl + 0.197 + 0.0592pH. The electrolyte used in both chambers was 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution which was purged with pure N2 or CO2 for 1 h before the electrochemical tests. sections.heading: 3.1 Morphological and structural characterization
sections.text:
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to characterize the morphology of the synthesized Cu_btc powders. As shown in Figure 1a-c, Cu_btc presented the octahedral structure with a relatively smooth surface, the average particle size was about 500 nm. The XRD indicated that all the diffraction peaks matched well with the simulated XRD pattern, 34 indicating the pure Cu_btc with good crystallinity (Figure 1i). Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA, Figure S1) of Cu_btc indicated three serious weight losses during the pyrolysis in N2 which were possibly ascribed to the volatilization of solvent, removal of residual water trapped in Cu_btc, and decomposition of organic linkers, respectively. Cu_btc structure began to decompose at 300 °C and no significant loss was detected after temperature higher than 400 °C. The carbonization of Cu_btc was conducted at 700, 800 and 900 °C for 5 h in Ar atmosphere. The morphology of the products after carbonization was showed in Figure 1 d, e and Figure S2. Most of the particles retained the geometric shape and size of Cu_btc but presented a wrinkled and rough surface. In order to explore the key factor for enhancing the selectivity for formate on
Cu2O/Cu@NC-800, the trend of maximal FEformate, the onset potential of CO2 electroreduction, and the nitrogen functionality content were plotted. As shown in
Figure 6b, the maximum FEformate showed a positive correlation with the Cu-N-Cu content, whereas no such trend was obtained for other N species. As the Cu-N-Cu

between the FEformate and the Cu-N-Cu content (Figure 6c and Table S7). It was proposed that the CO2 electroreduction involved in two significant intermediates: *OCHO and *COOH. The *OCHO mainly followed the pathway to generate formate,

Conclusion
In summary, Cu2O/Cu nanoparticles anchored into nitrogen-doped porous carbon frameworks (Cu2O/Cu@NC) with different features and N contents has been prepared by carbonizing Cu-btc at controlled temperatures. When carbonized at 800 °C, the
prepared catalyst (Cu2O/Cu@NC-800) exhibited a remarkable improvement of activity and selectivity towards formate as formate started to form at the low potential of –0.38
V versus Ag/AgCl and maximum faradic efficiencies for formate reached 70.5% at –
0.68 V. The better catalytic activities depended on the well dispersed metallic
nanoparticles in N-doped carbon frameworks and the formation of more low-index
facets which provided abundant reaction sites for CO2 adsorption and activation. Meanwhile, the higher content of N doped into the Cu2O lattice possibly facilitated *OCHO pathway by altering the electronic structure of Cu2O which lowered the binding energy of *OCHO to facilitate the formate production. Our research could give
new insights into the development of robust catalysts with superior activity and
selectivity for converting CO2 to formate.
